plan.contextChunk: This figure pairs two views of the same max-heap, labeled (a) on the left and (b) on the right. Panel (a) is a binary tree of ten gray circles joined by straight edges, with the value inside each circle and a smaller index printed just above and outside it. The root holds 16 at index 1; its children hold 14 at index 2 and 10 at index 3; the node 14 has children 8 at index 4 and 7 at index 5; the node 10 has children 9 at index 6 and 3 at index 7; the node 8 has children 2 at index 8 and 4 at index 9; and the node 7 has a single left child, 1 at index 10, so the bottom level is filled only from the left. Panel (b) is a horizontal row of ten gray boxes reading 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1 from left to right, with the indices 1 through 10 written above them. Curved arcs above and below the row connect each cell to the two cells that hold its children, which always lie further right. Setting the branching picture beside the flat row shows that the same parent-child relationships survive the change of representation. The figure introduces the array form of a heap, in which moving between a node and its children reduces to arithmetic on the index.

interactions.teaches: A tree node and its array cell are the same heap item, and clicking either representation reveals the corresponding parent and children in both views.

interactions.label: Index i
interactions.teaches: For any heap index i, simple arithmetic locates its relatives: floor(i/2) gives the parent, while 2i and 2i+1 give the children when those indices are within the heap size.

interactions.label: Overlay
interactions.teaches: The array layout records the tree's shape by position, while the max-heap property is a separate value rule requiring every parent to be at least as large as its children.

demo_steps.title: Two views of one heap
demo_steps.narration: The left panel shows the heap as a nearly complete binary tree, while the right panel stores the same nodes in array positions 1 through 10. The value sequence in the row is just the tree read level by level from left to right.

demo_steps.title: Navigate from an index
demo_steps.narration: Move the index slider to any cell or node. Its parent is at floor(i/2), and its children are at 2i and 2i+1 if those positions still fall inside the array.

demo_steps.title: Match tree nodes to array cells
demo_steps.narration: Click a node in the tree or a cell in the array to highlight the same item in both places. Its parent and children light up too, showing that the relationship is unchanged by the representation.

demo_steps.title: Separate shape from heap property
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the value-order overlay. The arcs still show the structure, but the emphasized comparisons now show the max-heap rule: each parent value is greater than or equal to each child value.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A heap array is not an arbitrary list: its indices encode the complete binary tree, so parent and child navigation becomes simple arithmetic.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Place the binary tree on the left and the array row on the right, matching the original two-panel composition. Use light gray filled circles for tree nodes and light gray filled rectangles for array cells, with black outlines and large black value labels. Put smaller index labels just above each node and above each array cell. The tree should be a nearly complete binary tree filled left to right, with node 10 as the left child of node 5 and no right child there. In the array panel, show values 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1 from left to right. Draw curved arcs between parent and child cells, alternating above and below the row as needed to reduce clutter. Structural overlay should emphasize arcs and corresponding indices; value-order overlay should emphasize parent-child comparisons such as 16 ≥ 14, 16 ≥ 10, 14 ≥ 8, and so on. Highlight selected item, parent, and children with distinct but coordinated colors so the mapping between tree and array is visually immediate.

authoredContext: The (binary) heap data structure is an array object that we can view as a nearly complete binary tree (see Section B.5.3), as shown in Figure 6.1. Each node of the tree corresponds to an element of the array. The tree is completely filled on all levels except possibly the lowest, which is filled from the left up to a point. An array A that represents a heap is an object with two attributes: A:length, which (as usual) gives the number of elements in the array, and A:heap-size, which represents how many elements in the heap are stored within array A.
